betterCitation: Oscar Wilde, Intentions, The Critic as Artist, Part II, 1891 (Gilbert)
reason: Attacked and survived, on the text itself rather than on a quotation site. The Wikisource page the evidence names would not give me the passage, so I pulled the whole of Intentions down as plain text from Project Gutenberg ebook 887 and searched it. There is exactly one occurrence of least himself in the book, and everything the proposal claims about it is confirmed by the surrounding lines. The heading A DIALOGUE: Part II stands above it, so Part II is right and not guessed. The nearest speaker label above it is GILBERT, opening the speech The difference between objective and subjective work is one of, exactly the speech the evidence names, and the next label after the sentence is ERNEST, so the sentence closes Gilbert's speech, which is what the locator says. The wording matches to the letter, including the preceding clause: Yes, the objective form is the most subjective in matter. Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth. No drift, no splice, nothing elided, and no translation in the way, since Wilde wrote in English. I checked the obvious alternative attribution and it fails: the mask is also the subject of The Truth of Masks in the same volume, and a careless citation would send the line there, but the text puts it in The Critic as Artist and the proposal has it in the right essay. It is not on the misattribution list; the Wilde entry there is Be yourself, everyone else is already taken, which is not Wilde at all and is a different line. Speaker is named, which the rule requires for a dialogue. Wilde is not banned, stands at zero of three for the year, and shipped.js returns no hit and no near-hit. Scope is clean: an 1891 dialogue printed in a book of essays, not scripture, not oratory, not a lyric, nothing needing a warning, and it is an aphorism, which is the month. Tag Essay is the form of the work, Intentions being a volume of essays, and the dialogue form does not make it Drama. The source line leads with the author's name, carries no dash, and runs 73 characters. Two things I would not refute but would tidy. The evidence names Osgood, McIlvaine, 1891 as the edition, but what I actually opened was the Gutenberg text of Intentions; the wording agrees, so the claim is true, but the edition line is stronger than the reading behind it. And the source puts the speaker parenthesis after the year rather than after the locator, which inverts the order the rule sets out; the form in betterCitation keeps work, locator, speaker in the order the rule gives and is three characters shorter. One thing the editor must watch, which is not a fault in this line: carry-in 03-cfl-10 is Oscar Wilde and its fitMonth is 5. Rule nine allows Wilde once in May, so the editor lands this or the Lady Windermere's Fan line, not both.
